title: Observability and SLOs
oneLiner: Logs, metrics and traces, then SLIs, SLOs, error budgets and burn-rate alerts, with the RED and USE methods for knowing what to measure.
keyTakeaway: Metrics tell you that something is wrong, traces tell you where, and logs tell you why. Define reliability from the user's side as an SLI (the share of good requests), set an SLO target below 100%, and treat the gap as an error budget you can spend on releases. Alert on how fast the budget is burning, not on every blip. For each service watch RED (rate, errors, duration); for each resource watch USE (utilization, saturation, errors).
explanation:
Observability is how well you can work out what a running system is doing from what it emits, without shipping new code to find out. It rests on three kinds of telemetry. Logs are records of individual events: a request failed, a job started. Structured logs (JSON fields rather than free text) can be searched and grouped, and every line should carry a correlation id (a request id passed along every hop) so you can collect everything one request did. Metrics are numbers aggregated over time: counters (requests served, which only go up), gauges (queue depth right now) and histograms (latency counts in buckets, from which percentiles are computed). They are cheap to keep for a long time and drive dashboards and alerts. Their cost is cardinality: every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series, so labelling a metric with user id creates millions of them. Traces follow one request across services. A trace is a tree of spans, each a timed operation (an HTTP call, a database query) with a parent, and the trace context travels between services in a header (the W3C standard is traceparent). OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for producing all three.

The usual workflow during an incident: an alert fires on a metric, a dashboard narrows it down (which endpoint, which region, which version), an example trace shows which span is slow or failing, and that span's logs show the error. Part 2 lets you read three traces and find the problem in each.

What to measure. The RED method, from Tom Wilkie, is for anything that serves requests: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests per second, or the share that fail) and Duration (latency, as a distribution). The USE method, from Brendan Gregg, is for resources such as CPUs, disks, network links, connection pools and queues: Utilization (how busy it is), Saturation (work waiting because it is full, such as run-queue length or pool waiters) and Errors. Google's SRE book calls latency, traffic, errors and saturation the four golden signals. Saturation is the early warning: latency stays flat until a resource is nearly full and then climbs steeply, as the Scale It Yourself lab shows.

SLIs, SLOs and SLAs. A service level indicator (SLI) is a measurement of what users experience, best written as a ratio of good events to all events: the share of requests that succeeded in under 300 ms, the share of minutes the checkout page loaded. A service level objective (SLO) is the target for that SLI over a window, such as 99.9% over 30 days. A service level agreement (SLA) is a contract with customers with penalties attached, set looser than the internal SLO so you find out before you owe anyone money. Measure as close to the user as you can: the load balancer's view of a request includes failures your application never logged.

The error budget is 100% minus the SLO. At 99.9% over 30 days, 0.1% of requests may fail; for availability measured in time, that is 43.2 minutes (30 days is 43,200 minutes). At 99.99% it is 4.3 minutes, which is less than most deploys take to roll back, so every extra nine is far more expensive than the last. The budget turns arguments into a rule: while there is budget left, ship features and take risks; when it is spent, slow releases down and work on reliability. 100% is the wrong target, because users can't tell 99.999% from 100% through their own flaky Wi-Fi, and chasing it stops all change.

Alert on burn rate. The burn rate is how fast you are using the budget compared with the steady pace that would use exactly all of it by the end of the window: the current error rate divided by the error rate the SLO allows. Burn rate 1 spends the budget in exactly 30 days; burn rate 14.4 spends 2% of it in an hour and all of it in about 2 days. The Google SRE Workbook suggests paging when 2% of a 30-day budget burns within an hour (burn rate 14.4) or 5% within 6 hours (burn rate 6), and opening a ticket when 10% burns within 3 days (burn rate 1), each confirmed by a short window so the alert stops soon after the problem does. Paging on "error rate above 1% for 5 minutes" instead wakes people for blips that never threatened the SLO and misses slow leaks that do.

Part 1 is an error budget and burn rate calculator, Part 2 three traces to diagnose, and Part 3 a quick sort of metrics into RED and USE.
